items.question_en: Consider a gas with molar mass M. If the sound at frequency f is introduced to a tube of this gas at temperature T then an internal acoustic standing wave is set up with nodes separated by L. The adiabatic constant (γ = Cp/Cv) is

solution.approach: The speed of sound in the gas from the standing wave equals the speed from the adiabatic gas formula, since the node separation gives the wavelength.

steps.text: Write the speed of sound in a gas of adiabatic constant γ.
Relate the node separation to the wavelength. Successive nodes of a standing wave are half a wavelength apart.
Write the wave speed from the frequency and this wavelength.
Equate the two expressions for v and square both sides.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the node separation L itself as the full wavelength (forgetting nodes are half a wavelength apart), giving v = fL and γ = Mf²L²/RT.
Inverting the node-separation relation as L = 2λ instead of λ = 2L, giving λ = L/2, v = fL/2, and γ = Mf²L²/4RT.

concept_tags: speed of sound in a gas

items.question_en: A wave is represented by the equation y = (0.02 m) sin(5πx − 20t). The minimum distance between the two particles always having the same speed is. (Assume x and t are in SI units)

solution.approach: Two particles have the same speed at every instant only if their phases differ by a whole multiple of π, and the smallest such separation is half a wavelength.

steps.text: Find the particle velocity by differentiating the displacement with respect to time.
Find the wavelength from the coefficient of x.
State when two particles keep the same speed magnitude for all time. Their phases differ by Δ, and |cos(θ+Δ)| = |cos θ| for every θ only when Δ is a whole multiple of π.
steps.why_this_step: cos(θ+Δ) reduces to ±cos θ for every θ only when sin Δ = 0, which needs Δ = nπ.

steps.text: Take the smallest nonzero multiple of π and convert it to a distance using Δ = k(x₁ − x₂).
steps.equation: Δ = π = k·d, so d = π/k = λ/2

common_mistakes.text: Requiring the velocity to match in direction as well as magnitude, which needs a full wavelength separation, giving 0.4 m.
Multiplying the wavelength by 2 instead of dividing it by 2, giving 0.8 m instead of 0.2 m.

items.question_en: An observer moves towards a stationary source of sound with a speed (1/5)th that of sound. The frequency of the sound emitted by the source is f. The apparent frequency recorded by the observer is

solution.approach: For an observer moving towards a stationary source, the apparent frequency increases by the ratio of the sum of the wave speed and the observer's speed to the wave speed.

steps.text: Write the Doppler formula for a source at rest and an observer moving towards it with speed v_o.
Substitute the observer's speed as one fifth of the speed of sound.

common_mistakes.text: Using the minus sign as if the observer were moving away from the source, giving f(v − v/5)/v = 0.8f.
Assuming the frequency does not change because the source itself is at rest, ignoring the observer's own motion.
Ignoring the one-fifth fraction and taking the observer's speed as equal to the speed of sound, giving f(v + v)/v = 2f.

items.question_en: A wave is given by the equation y = (0.02) sin(πx − 8πt) then the velocity of the wave is (y and x are in metre and t is in second)

solution.approach: The wave speed is the ratio of the angular frequency to the wave number, read directly from the coefficients of t and x.

steps.text: Identify the wave number and the angular frequency from the equation.
steps.equation: y = 0.02 sin(πx − 8πt), so k = π rad m⁻¹, ω = 8π rad s⁻¹

steps.text: Find the wave speed from the ratio of angular frequency to wave number.

common_mistakes.text: Computing the frequency f = ω/2π = 4 Hz and the wavelength λ = 2π/k = 2 m correctly, then doubling the product to get v = 2fλ = 16 ms⁻¹.
Dividing the wave number by the angular frequency instead of the other way round, giving v = π/8π = 0.125 ms⁻¹, which matches no option.
